## Methods

Chemical materials
KOH (AR, 95%), Ni(SO4)·6H2O (AR, 98%), Ni(NO3)2·6H2O (AR, 98%), Fe(NO3)3·9H2O (AR, 98%), and Co(NO3)2·6H2O (AR, 99%) were purchased from Shanghai Hushi Company. (NH4)6Mo7O24·4H2O (AR, 99%), ethanol (C2H5OH, AR), and isopropanol (C3H8O, AR) were purchased from Shanghai Bide Pharm Company. Nickel foam was obtained from Suzhou Xingzhenghong Company. 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF, 99%) was obtained from Zhejiang Sugar Energy Company, and 5-formyl-2-furancarboxylic acid (FFCA, 98%) was obtained from Shanghai Titan Company. 5-hydroxymethylfurancarboxylic acid (HMFCA, 98%) and 2,5-diformylfuran (DFF, 98%) were purchased from Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc. 2,5-furandicarboxylic acid (FDCA, 99%) was obtained from Shanghai Meryer Chemical Technology Co., Ltd. PAP-TP-85 (A40, a terphenyl-based poly(aryl piperidinium) polymer) was purchased from Suzhou Sinero Technology Co., Ltd.

Catalyst and polymer preparation
Preparation of Ni-Co/NF catalyst: a piece of Nickel foam (NF, 1.0 mm thickness, 5.0 × 5.2 cm2) was cut and washed in 3.0 M HCl for 30 minutes, followed by ultrasonication in ethanol and acetone for 30 minutes, respectively. After that, the NF was vertically immersed in a 100 mL aqueous solution (75 mL deionized H2O and 25 mL isopropanol), which consists of 17.55 mmol NiSO4·6H2O and 4.95 mmol Co(NO3)2·6H2O. The above solution containing NF was maintained at 40 °C for 24 h. Next, the catalyst was taken out and washed three times with deionized H2O and isopropanol. Then, it was aged in a 1.0 M KOH solution at 60 °C for 8 h. Finally, the catalyst was taken out and rinsed with deionized H2O three times, denoted as Ni-Co/NF. The mass loading of 2.7 ± 0.1 mg cm−2 was determined by measuring the NF weight before and after immersion. Preparation of Ni(OH)2/NF, Co(OH)2/NF and Co(OH)2/CF catalysts: NF (5.0 × 5.2 cm2) was immersed in the aqueous solutions containing 22.5 mmol of NiSO4·6H2O and Co(NO3)2·6H2O, respectively, to prepare Ni(OH)2/NF and Co(OH)2/NF via an impregnation strategy similar to that used for the Ni-Co catalyst (same preparation temperature and duration). The pretreatment method for cobalt foam (CF, 5.0 × 5.2 cm2) was consistent with that for NF, and the Co(OH)2/CF catalyst was also prepared by the identical impregnation method in a solution with 22.5 mmol Co(NO3)2·6H2O. Preparation of Ni-Fe/NF catalyst: 2.13 mmol Ni(NO3)2·6H2O and 0.71 mmol Fe(NO3)3·9H2O were dissolved in 30 mL deionized H2O with 10 mL ethanol. A washed NF (2.0 × 2.0 cm2) was immersed in the above solution at room temperature for 24 h. The catalyst was taken out and washed three times with ethanol and deionized H2O. After drying in an oven, the obtained catalyst on NF was denoted as Ni-Fe/NF. Preparation of Ni-Mo/NF catalyst: a washed NF (5.0 × 5.2 cm2) was immersed in 200 mL deionized H2O with 2.70 mmol (NH4)6Mo7O24·4H2O and 10.80 mmol Ni(NO3)2·6H2O. Next, the solution containing NF was transferred to a Teflon-lined autoclave at 150 °C for 6 h to obtain the catalyst precursor. The obtained precursor was washed with deionized H2O and ethanol, then dried under vacuum. Afterward, it was calcinated in an H2/Ar (v/v=5/95) atmosphere at 500 °C for 2 h to prepare the Ni-Mo/NF catalyst. Polymerization of polyethylene furanoate (PEF): 23.4 g of obtained FDCA (0.15 mol), 18.6 g of ethylene glycol (0.30 mol), and tetrabutyl titanate (TBT) as the catalyst (500 ppm of the total monomer mass), were vigorously stirred at 150 °C for 30 min in a 100 mL three-necked flask. Next, the temperature is raised to 180–200 °C for condensation polymerization. When the mass of collected water reached 95% of the theoretical water yield, the polycondensation process was complete. The reaction temperature was then increased to 210 °C for pre-polymerization, which lasted 1–1.5 h. Subsequently, the temperature was raised to 220–230 °C for terminal polymerization. When a pronounced pole-climbing phenomenon was observed, the reaction was finished.

Material and flow channel characterizations
Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) was performed with Cu Kα (0.154 nm) radiation on a Bruker D8 Advance X-ray diffractometer. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM) images and Energy-dispersive X-ray (EDS) mappings were obtained on a Talos F200X G2 electron microscope operating at an accelerating voltage of 200 kV. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images were collected by an analytical field emission scanning electron microscope (ZEISS, Germini 450). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements were performed on a Micro-focus X-ray photoelectron spectrometer (Thermo Scientific, Nexsa G2). Proton nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR) measurement was carried out on an NMR Spectrometer (Bruker BioSpin, AVANCE NEO). Three-dimensional images of the flow channel structure were collected by a confocal laser scanning microscope (ZEISS, LSM 900). The pressure distribution tests were conducted using a flexible pressure sensor (CNSCAN, G-Scan).

Electrochemical measurements
All three-electrode electrochemical tests were performed using an electrochemical workstation (Metrohm, Autolab PGSTAT302N with 10 A current booster) in a divided H-type cell at ambient temperature, unless otherwise stated. The prepared catalysts (1 × 1 cm2), Hg/HgO, and Pt mesh (2 × 2 cm2) were used as the working, reference, and counter electrodes (internal resistance obtained from the Nyquist plot). Both cathode and anode chambers were filled with 20 mL 1.0 M KOH (pH 13.67 ± 0.15) and separated by an anion exchange membrane (AEM, PAP-TP-85, 40 μm). AEM was pretreated with 1 M KOH for 12 h. Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) was measured at a scan rate of 5 mV s−1 without iR correction. The electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) tests were performed with a frequency range from 100 kHz to 0.1 Hz with an amplitude of 10 mV. All potentials were converted to reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) through the following equation: ERHE = Emeasured + 0.098 + 0.0591 × pH.

AEM-HMFOR electrolyzer performance tests
The AEM-HMFOR electrolyzer includes end plates (PEEK), polar plates (high-purity Ni, ≥99.99%), and MEA. The MEA takes Ni-Co/NF as the anode, Ni-Mo/NF as the cathode, and PAP-TP-85 as the membrane (internal resistance obtained from the Nyquist curve). For multi-batch electrolysis, the anolyte was fed 1.0 M KOH with 0.2 M HMF (20 mL), and the catholyte was fed 1.0 M KOH (20 mL). The HMF conversion efficiency of the AEM-HMFOR electrolyzer was evaluated by chronoamperometry (CA) tests at selected cell voltages. In single-pass mode, the stability of the stacks was investigated by chronopotentiometry (CP) using an electrochemical workstation (100 A current booster) at selected currents. All electrolyzer operating conditions are summarized in Table S14.

Product analysis
Quantitative and qualitative analyses of the products were determined by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) with a C-18 column (Shim-pack GWS, 4.6 × 100 mm, 5 μm) and a UV-Vis detector set at 265 nm. The eluent consisted of 5 mM ammonium formate and methanol in a volume ratio of 4:1 at a flow rate of 0.5 mL min−1 for 10 min. The 100 μL electrolyte obtained during electrolysis was diluted 1000-fold (initial HMF concentration of 200 mM), 2000-fold (400 mM), and 4000-fold (500 mM) with ultrapure H2O for HPLC analysis. The single-pass conversion efficiency (SPCE) of HMF, space-time yield (STY) of FDCA, Faradaic efficiency (FE), specific energy consumption (SEC), and FDCA yield were calculated by the following equations:
SPCEHMF = mol of HMF consumed / mol of initial HMF × 100%
STYFDCA = mass of FDCA produced / (geometric area of anode × electrolysis time)
FEFDCA = mol FDCA produced × 6 × F / Q × 100%
YieldFDCA = mol of FDCA produced / mol of initial HMF × 100%
SEC = Ustack × Istack / FDCA productivity, (Unit: kWh kg−1)
where F refers to the Faraday constant (96,485 C mol−1) and Q is the passed charge.

Data availability
The data supporting the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request. Source data are provided with this paper.

### Reviewer 2

This study proposes a green electrochemical process for producing FDCA from biomass-derived HMF via an anion-exchange membrane–based oxidation reaction (AEM-HMFOR), achieving a high Faradaic efficiency (94.6%) and FDCA yield (96.2%) with high purity. In addition, the authors demonstrate the techno-economic and environmental feasibility of the process through comprehensive TEA and LCA. Notably, the proposed system achieves a production cost of approximately $2,300/ton and significantly lower global warming potential compared to conventional FDCA production. Overall, this work offers a promising direction for replacing fossil-derived plastics with biomass-based alternatives. However, several issues must be addressed before this manuscript is suitable for publication in Nature Communications.
1. The authors should clarify the specific advantages of the AEM-HMFOR process over conventional chemical-catalytic oxidation routes in terms of selectivity, operational conditions, environmental impacts, and potential for coupling with renewable electricity.
2. While chemical oxidation processes typically benefit from economies of scale, the scalability of membrane-based systems such as AEM-HMFOR may face limitations due to membrane cost, durability, and stack integration complexity. The authors should discuss how such scale effects may impact the long-term competitiveness of the proposed system at commercial scale.
3. The authors mentioned on page 11 that 3 M H₂SO₄ was used to neutralize unreacted KOH prior to membrane separation, whereas Figure 5c shows neutralization occurring after the RO membrane. This discrepancy should be clarified to avoid confusion regarding process flow.
4. Given that HMF and KOH are the dominant contributors to both economic cost and environmental impact, a sensitivity analysis with respect to their price and GWP assumptions is recommended. This would enhance the robustness of the TEA and LCA conclusions.
5. Since both input and output scales linearly with plant capacity, the claim that a larger separation system lowers GWP per kg of FDCA may not be fully justified. The authors should explain whether improved energy efficiency or other nonlinear effects contribute to the reduced GWP.
6. The prices listed in Table S8 are mostly retail prices from chemical suppliers, which are not representative of bulk industrial pricing. The authors should provide or estimate wholesale prices for a fair comparison with their proposed production cost.
7. The current TEA includes equipment and operating costs but omits overheads such as labor, financing, depreciation, and discount rate. These are crucial for realistic comparison with commercial FDCA prices and should at least be discussed as limitations.

The authors specified that the data collected is from recent publications without further specification. Yet, there appears to be some data missing (e.g. 10.1021/acsenergylett.4c03257 – 200mM HMF, 83 mg/cm²/h, or 10.1021/acssuschemeng.4c04754 – 1M HMF, 140mg/cm²/h.). It is advised to revisit the data included or specify the basis on which data was curated.
4) Visibility of Data for Charge Transfer resistance (Rct)
On page 5 line one the authors describe the Rct from Figure S5. However, due to the large dots in Figure S5, it is hard to distinguish individual lines/data points. Revisiting and redesigning (e.g. smaller dots/excerpt) the figure is recommended.
5) Missing Information/accessibility of methods:
The authors test different flow channel widths; however, the flowrate is not apparent, neither in the method section in the SI, nor in the manuscript. It could be the same as for Figure 3, but specification is needed.
Further, the “three-electrode system” (page 4 line 28) is not described in the methods, it needs to be specified if this is an H-cell, beaker or flow-cell.
For example, a table in the SI that links the results of the (sub) Figures to the experimental conditions (such as electrode are, CA or CP, current/voltage applied, flow rate, electrolyte, charge for evaluation, …) could increase accessibility.
6) Inconsistency in data interpretation:
On page 6 line 11 and following, the authors claim that HMF concentrations above 200mM lead to AEM degradation and increasing ohmic losses. However, this is not apparent in Figure S5 and its interpretation on page 5 line 1. Further, this conclusion is not mentioned when regarding elevated concentrations for the 100cm2 electrolyzer and its implications for elevated HMF concentrations.
7) Calculation of activation energy with reference to Figure 3a.
The authors show the resulting cell voltage in Figure 3a with and without flow channels. The general result is plausible. Yet, for the 200 mV difference (displayed in Figure 3a) the main single contributor is the higher activation potential in Figure S14, which is not specified in the manuscript. Clarification on why the activation potential changes with the addition of flow channels is required.
8) Clarification on Error Bars in Figure 3b:
Figure 3b is the only figure with error bars (for STY and FE) – clarification on what these display (and the absence of error bars on yield) is necessary.
9) Missing current profile for Figure 3c:
The authors provide an STY for different flow rates after identical charge has passed through the electrode. The resulting STY (at roughly equal FE) can only result from increasing current. Since the difference is very high between 0.25 and 1 ml/min, displaying the current/time plots for these graphs in the SI would be beneficial as it is only implicitly given in the current form. Further, if the electrolyzer is “undersupplied” with HMF at low flow rates, this should be mentioned as, in this case, the reason would not be mass transfer limitations but the absence of HMF in the electrolyzer.
10) Altering charge as basis for evaluation.
The authors evaluated the experiments in Figure 3b and Figure 3c after different charges (2000 C and 2300 C) in Figure 3. Clarification on why these points were chosen is necessary. Further, Figure 3c is the only such diagram that lacks the FDCA yield, which should be included.
11) Voltage-Yield relation inconsistency/Electrical resistance in P-Stack:
On page 8 line 4, (Figure S20) the authors describe the lowered FE at elevated voltage (above 1.6V), which they attributed to OER, which is plausible. Yet, in Figure 4f, the authors describe, show how a cell voltage of 1.8 and ~2V produces a yield and FE of close to 100%. This inconsistency needs to be mentioned, and the phenomenon needs to be described. The “internal resistance” of the P-stack needs to be described and measured in more detail. Contact resistance needs to be accounted for at the elevated current and actual current distribution should be measured in the individual cells. This could give an indication of HMF conversion in the individual compartments.
12) Clarification on differences and comparison between S-Stack and P-Stack:
On page 9 line 5 and following the authors describe how in the S-stack the electrolyte flows similar to an electrolyzer without a flow-channel, while in the P-stack, the electrolyte flowed as in an electrolyzer with a flow channel. However, the authors do not sufficiently make clear why this is the case. It should be clarified whether there are flow channels in both electrolyzers and why the flow is different (possibly via a sketch in the SI). If there are significant differences, they should be named. Furthermore, a fair comparison should be made.
The comparison is also hindered by the flow-velocity in both stacks. The flow rate in the P-stack is 5 times higher than in the S-stack (page 9 line 11). This would result in an actual flow velocity that is 27 times as high as in the S-stack (5*7,18/1,33) as there is a sequential flow in the P-stack while (as in a longer tube) than in the S-stack (as in a wider tube through parallel flow cells). This would result in vastly different mass transfer properties. Here, clarification and reevaluation of the comparison, especially in reference to the results in Figure 3c is necessary.
13) Potentially misleading comparison on setups in Figure 5b):
The Spider-web diagram in Figure 5b is somewhat misleading in terms of SEC. For all other metrics, the favorable number are on the outside, while for the SEC, it would be more favorable to be at the center. This implies a superior performance of the 80A setup, while in terms of SEC, this is not the case. Therefore, this metric should be reconsidered and could be replaced by e.g. the amount of FDCA produced per kWh.
14) Additional information required on lower flowrate threshold:
On page 9 line 23, the authors mention that a lower flowrate can destabilize electrocatalysis which is a highly interesting finding for practical application. If there is additional information on this (e.g. threshold value regarding current density), the scientific community would benefit much from sharing this information.
15) Missing information on FDCA purification process:
The authors purified FDCA from the solution, which is highly relevant for industrial application. However, the manuscript lacks information on the purification procedure. To be able to reproduce the underlying data for the subsequent TEA and LCA, it is necessary to report on the membranes (pore size/MWCO and supplier) and membrane area used, the pressure difference, and the stage-cut of the individual stages (both NF and RO). This is highly relevant to judge whether water can be recycled and how energy-intense the separation would be. Further, the pH of the product solution should be measured, as close to 0.5M of FDCA (with two carboxylic acid groups) should have a substantial influence on the pH of the solution.
16) Lack of discussion on PEF quality:
The authors report on the color of PEF when polymerized from purified FDCA (page 11 line 20). While it is clear that an extensive analysis of the PEF quality is beyond the scope of this work, the authors should include the necessity for future analysis, especially regarding critical impurities that might require different purification steps.
17) TEA:
a. The authors state that even at current market prices, the AEM-HMFOR system would achieve reasonable profits (page 13 line 4). However, the products would remain in solution (in 1.2M KOH, according to the caption of Figure S34), which would not be the specification in Table S8. Here, clarification is needed. Further, the y-axis of Figure S34 does not match the numbers in Note S8 and the manuscript. This should be revised.
b. While the authors design a system to purify FDCA, in the TEA the authors assume purification costs to be 30% of the electrolyzer costs. If there is a reason the authors do not refer to their purification system, it should be discussed, otherwhise, the designed system should be used as a basis for the TEA, as it is for the LCA.
c. Additionally, other costs (such as that the MEA costs 3% of the electrolyzer and the MEA will run as long as the electrolyzer) are assumed without a reference indication. This would be necessary for clarification. Further, a discussion on the uncertainty of these assumptions is necessary.
d. In the SI, the authors calculate an offset for H2 and K2SO4 price but do not specify whether this is included in the FDCA costs or if it is neglected. Especially the K2SO4 prices will have a significant influence. Yet, it can only be discussed in combination with the purification steps. Furthermore, paired electrolysis should be mentioned as a possibility to increase the economic perspectives (e.g. 10.1021/acssuschemeng.3c03144, 10.1021/acssuschemeng.4c04754 or 10.1039/D1GC00914A)
e. The color choice in graph Figure 5e makes distinguishing between H2O and KOH costs fairly difficult, a line connecting KOH with the respective part in the diagram could assist.
18) LCA:
The authors provide numbers on FDCA GWP and other factors which is highly relevant. In the discussion of these numbers, a comparison to similar products (e.g. Terephthalic acid as a precursor for PET) should be made to give a perspective to the numbers calculated.
19) General lack of presentation of cathode side:
In all Figures except Figure 1c, there is no input of water on the cathode side on all diagrams. Additionally, there is a lack of data in the method section on the cathode side of the experiment. It is advised to clarify H2 production and the supply of water to the system, since OH- ions are supplied through the AEM. Furthermore, there is no mentioning of cation leakage through the AEM. If this was not measured, the possibility should at least be mentioned in the discussion.
20) In the SI, Reference 6 and 7 appear to be identical.
If these comments can be satisfied, a publication can be recommended.
